questions.q: When a vector R is resolved into its horizontal and vertical component vectors using its polar angle \(\theta\), what are the magnitudes of those two perpendicular components?
options: \(R_x = R\sin\theta\) and \(R_y = R\cos\theta\)
\(R_x = R\cos\theta\) and \(R_y = R\sin\theta\)
\(R_x = R\tan\theta\) and \(R_y = R/\cos\theta\)
\(R_x = R\cos\theta\) and \(R_y = R\cos\theta\)
questions.explanation: Using the polar angle measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component is \(R_x = R\cos\theta\) (adjacent, so cosine) and the vertical component is \(R_y = R\sin\theta\) (opposite, so sine). The classic error is swapping them: from the horizontal, horizontal is cosine.

questions.q: When adding several vectors by perpendicular components, you first add all the horizontal components to find Rx and all the vertical components to find Ry. How do you then obtain the magnitude and angle of the resultant R?
options: Add Rx and Ry as scalars to get the magnitude, then halve it for the angle
Use Pythagoras's theorem to find the magnitude of R, then use trigonometry to find the angle \(\theta\)
Use the cosine rule for the angle and the sine rule for the magnitude
Multiply Rx by Ry to get the magnitude, then take the inverse sine for the angle
questions.explanation: After summing the horizontal components (Rx) and the vertical components (Ry), Pythagoras's theorem gives the magnitude of the resultant R and trigonometry (the inverse tangent of Ry over Rx) gives the angle \(\theta\). Never add vector magnitudes as scalars.

questions.q: When two displacement vectors are added graphically, the labelled arrows are placed head to tail. Where is the resultant vector drawn?
options: From the head of the first vector to the tail of the second vector
From the tail of the first vector to the head of the second (last) vector
From the midpoint of the first vector to the midpoint of the second
Parallel to the longer of the two vectors, with length equal to their sum
questions.explanation: Placed head to tail, the sum of the vectors is the arrow drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector. The order in which the vectors are added does not change the resultant.

questions.q: To carry out the vector subtraction \(v - u\) (for example when finding a change in velocity), how is the vector \(-u\) constructed and combined?
options: \(-u\) is half the magnitude of \(u\) and is added head to tail to \(v\)
\(-u\) is equal in magnitude to \(u\) but directed in the opposite direction, and is added to \(v\)
\(-u\) is perpendicular to \(u\) and is subtracted from \(v\)
\(-u\) is the same as \(u\), and the two are simply added as scalars
questions.explanation: The vector subtraction \(v - u\) is achieved by adding the inverse vector \(-u\) to \(v\). The vector \(-u\) is equal in magnitude to \(u\) but is directed in the opposite direction. In the episode, 'minus twenty east' becomes 'plus twenty west' — reverse and add.

questions.q: The syllabus requires you to analyse the relative motion of objects in two dimensions. Which set of situations does it name as examples?
options: A ball rolling down a ramp, a pendulum swinging, and a spinning wheel
The motion of a boat on a flowing river, the motion of two moving cars, and the motion of an aeroplane in a crosswind
A satellite in orbit, a projectile launched at an angle, and a car braking
A swimmer in a still pool, a stationary kite, and a parked plane
questions.explanation: The inquiry question lists the motion of a boat on a flowing river, two moving cars, and an aeroplane in a crosswind. All three are solved by the same rule: the velocity of A relative to B is the vector subtraction \(v_A - v_B\).

questions.q: A car travels 4.0 km north and then 6.0 km west. Using Pythagoras's theorem, calculate the magnitude of its displacement.
questions.given: Two perpendicular legs: 4.0 km north and 6.0 km west
working: The two legs are perpendicular, so the displacement is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.
questions.explanation: Because the legs are perpendicular, the magnitude is found with Pythagoras (not by adding 4 + 6 = 10). The full displacement is a vector, so the direction \(56.3^\circ\) west of north must also be stated.

questions.q: A cyclist travels due east for 4 km before turning 60° towards the south and then continuing for a further 8 km. Using the cosine rule, calculate the magnitude of the cyclist's displacement.
questions.given: Leg 1 = 4 km east, leg 2 = 8 km at 60° towards the south; interior angle between the legs = 120°
working: The interior angle between the 4 km and 8 km vectors is \(180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ\).
Direction from the sine rule: \(\theta = 40.9^\circ\) south of west, so \(s = 10.58\,\mathrm{km}\) at \(40.9^\circ\) south of west.
questions.explanation: When the two vectors are not perpendicular, the cosine rule gives the magnitude and the sine rule gives the angle. Here the included angle is 120°, and \(\cos 120^\circ = -0.5\) makes the displacement larger than either leg alone.

questions.q: From memory: what is relative velocity, and what is the equation for the velocity of object A relative to object B?
keyPoints: Relative velocity is the velocity of an object as measured by a moving observer.
The velocity of A relative to B is found from the velocities of A and B relative to a stationary frame of reference.
\(v_{A\,\mathrm{rel}\,B} = v_A - v_B\) — a vector subtraction, not a scalar one.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that it is the velocity seen by a moving observer and gave \(v_{A\,\mathrm{rel}\,B} = v_A - v_B\), grade yourself Good or Easy. In two dimensions the subtraction is done with components or a vector triangle, but the rule is identical.

questions.q: In your own words: why do perpendicular components being independent mean a boat pointed straight across a flowing river takes the same time to cross whether or not the river is flowing?
keyPoints: The crossing time depends only on the component of velocity across the river and the width of the river.
The current acts purely downstream, perpendicular to the across direction, so it has no across-the-river component.
Because perpendicular components are independent, the current changes where the boat lands (further downstream) but not when it arrives.
This same independence of perpendicular components is the foundation of projectile motion next year.
questions.explanation: If you linked the crossing time to the across component only, and said the perpendicular current adds nothing to that component, grade yourself Good or Easy. This independence is the single most important idea in two-dimensional motion.

questions.q: A boat points straight across a river and travels at 4 m s⁻¹ relative to the water, while the river flows at 3 m s⁻¹ downstream. Determine the boat's resultant velocity relative to the bank, and outline the response structure a marker rewards. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The boat's velocity across the water (4 m s⁻¹) and the river's downstream velocity (3 m s⁻¹) are perpendicular, so they combine as a right-angled vector triangle. The magnitude of the resultant is \(\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The direction is the angle downstream of straight across, \(\tan^{-1}(3/4) \approx 37^\circ\). So the boat travels at 5 m s⁻¹ at about 37° downstream of straight across. The strong answer states the velocities are perpendicular, uses Pythagoras for the magnitude, finds the angle with the inverse tangent, and gives both magnitude AND direction, because velocity is a vector.

criteria.descriptor: Treats the two velocities as perpendicular vectors and uses Pythagoras to get 5 m s⁻¹.
Finds the direction using the inverse tangent of the downstream component over the across component (≈ 37°).
States both magnitude and direction; does not just add 4 + 3 = 7 as scalars.

questions.explanation: A weak answer adds the magnitudes (4 + 3 = 7) or gives a speed with no direction. Vectors add as vectors: perpendicular 3 and 4 make 5, and the final velocity answer must carry its direction.
